prompt.1: Oil and gas create jobs, but they also add to climate change. What should BC do?
prompt.2: BC sells natural gas, but it is behind on its goal to cut the gases that warm the climate. What should it do?
prompt.3: What direction should BC take on climate change and energy?
prompt.4: Which direction should BC take on climate targets, carbon pricing for industry and natural gas production?
prompt.5: Choose a direction on emissions targets, industrial carbon pricing, liquefied natural gas (LNG) expansion and clean power.

context.1: Oil and gas bring jobs and money to BC, but burning them adds to climate change. In 2025 the government stopped the carbon tax people paid on fuel. Big industry still pays a carbon charge. Parties disagree on gas exports, oil pipelines and climate goals.
context.2: In 2025 BC stopped charging the carbon tax on the fuel people buy, but large industries still pay a carbon price. The province is also allowing more plants that export natural gas. BC expects to cut its climate pollution by only half of what the law requires by 2030.
context.3: BC expects to cut its climate pollution 20% by 2030, which is half of the 40% target set in law. The carbon tax that people paid on fuel ended in 2025, but large industries still pay a carbon price. Parties disagree on growing natural gas exports, on oil pipelines and on whether to keep the carbon price for industry.
context.4: BC's emissions are projected to be 20% below 2007 levels by 2030, while the law sets a 40% target. In 2025 the NDP government ended the consumer carbon tax and the rebates for electric vehicles, and in 2026 it cut the 2035 target for zero-emission new car sales from 100% to 75%. Carbon pricing for large industry and clean fuel rules remain. LNG Canada, a liquefied natural gas (LNG) export project, approved its Phase 2 expansion in September 2026.
context.5: BC law set targets of 16% below 2007 emissions by 2025 and 40% by 2030, but the 2025 accountability report projects cuts of only 2.6% and 20%. The consumer carbon tax has been zero since April 1, 2025. The Output-Based Pricing System, which charges large industrial emitters and tightens 1% a year, remains. So does the Low Carbon Fuel Standard, which requires a 30% cut in the carbon intensity of fuels by 2030. Electric vehicle rebates ended, and in April 2026 the 2035 zero-emission vehicle sales target was cut from 100% to 75%. LNG Canada made its final investment decision on Phase 2 in September 2026. An oil pipeline to the coast, called Pacific Link, has been proposed.

text.1: Produce as much oil and gas as possible, and drop climate charges and goals.
text.2: Produce as much oil and gas as possible, stop charging industry for pollution, and drop climate targets.
text.3: Maximize oil and gas, end carbon pricing for industry, and drop climate targets.
text.4: Approve a pipeline to the coast, end industrial carbon pricing, the clean fuel rules and the CleanBC climate plan, and abandon the 2030 target.
text.5: Build a pipeline to Prince Rupert or Kitimat, repeal the industrial carbon price and the Low Carbon Fuel Standard, wind down CleanBC, and set no emissions targets.

text.1: Sell much more natural gas overseas and end the province's climate plan, but keep the carbon charge on big industry.
text.2: Sell much more natural gas abroad, scrap the province's climate plan and electric car sales rule, keep the carbon price on big industry, and set no new targets.
text.3: Expand natural gas exports quickly, repeal the CleanBC climate plan and the electric vehicle sales rule, keep the industrial carbon price, and set no new climate targets.
text.4: Double gas output by 2032 and triple it by 2035, repeal CleanBC and the zero-emission vehicle sales quota, keep the industrial carbon price and its revenue, and count emissions avoided by gas exports.
text.5: Double gas by 2032 and triple it by 2035, approve pipelines to the coast, repeal CleanBC and the zero-emission vehicle sales quota, keep the industrial carbon price, count emissions avoided abroad by cleaner exports, and set no new targets.

text.1: Sell more natural gas, keep climate charges on big industry, and build clean power.
text.2: Keep building gas export plants that run on clean power, keep industry's pollution charges, and add wind power.
text.3: Expand gas export plants built to reach net-zero emissions, keep carbon pricing for industry, and build clean power.
text.4: Keep industrial carbon pricing and clean fuel rules with no consumer tax, grow net-zero-ready liquefied natural gas, and build wind power and power lines.
text.5: Keep the consumer carbon tax at zero and the industrial carbon price and clean fuel standard, grow net-zero-ready gas exports to 48 million tonnes a year, fund a $36 billion grid, and keep the 2030 target.

text.1: Stop new oil and gas projects, and spend on clean power instead.
text.2: Approve no new gas, oil or pipeline projects, and fund clean power and energy-saving home upgrades.
text.3: Allow no new fossil fuel projects or pipeline, and fund renewable power and home energy upgrades.
text.4: Allow no new fossil fuel projects or pipeline, make gas exporters pay for their own power, end fossil fuel subsidies, and expand home energy upgrades.
text.5: Allow no new fossil fuel development or pipeline, make gas exporters pay for their own power, end fossil fuel subsidies, and make electricity 35% of energy use by 2035.

text.1: Set a lower climate goal, keep charging big polluters, and help homes save energy.
text.2: Set a lower climate goal BC can meet, keep charging big industry, and lend money for home energy upgrades.
text.3: Lower the 2030 target in law to a 20% cut, keep industrial carbon pricing, pass a methane law, and offer home-upgrade loans.
text.4: Set a 2030 milestone of 20% below 2007 in law, keep industrial carbon pricing, pass a methane law, offer $500 million in home-upgrade loans, add highway chargers, and keep the tanker ban.
text.5: Legislate a 2030 milestone of 20% below 2007, keep the 2040 and 2050 targets and the industrial carbon price, cut methane 75% by 2030, lend $500 million for home retrofits, and keep the tanker ban.

text.1: This party ended the carbon tax on fuel people buy, but it keeps carbon charges on big industry and is growing gas exports. It also promises money for home heat pumps and electric car chargers.
text.3: In government, the NDP ended the consumer carbon tax and rebates for electric vehicles, approved more liquefied natural gas and kept carbon pricing for industry. It admits BC will miss its 2030 target by about half and has not said how it will respond. On October 13 it promised $50 million a year for heat pumps, $16 million a year for electric vehicle chargers and a goal to nearly eliminate methane emissions by 2035.
text.5: The NDP cut the consumer carbon tax to zero in April 2025 but kept the industrial carbon price and the Low Carbon Fuel Standard. It ended electric vehicle rebates, cut the 2035 zero-emission vehicle sales target from 100% to 75%, and signed wind power contracts. BC is projected to reach 20% below 2007 by 2030, against 40% in law. For 2026 it promises more liquefied natural gas, a north coast transmission line and a temporary 10 cent per litre fuel tax cut. It would accept a pipeline only if the tanker ban stays. Its October 13 climate plan adds $50 million a year for heat pump rebates, $16 million a year to triple public EV charging ports over a decade, $4 million a year to double the Youth Climate Corps, and a pledge to meet the 75% methane cut by 2030 and 'virtually eliminate methane emissions by 2035'.

text.1: This party wants to sell much more natural gas abroad and end the climate plan, but keep the carbon charge on big industry.
text.3: The Conservatives would double gas output by 2032, approve LNG plants and pipelines, repeal the CleanBC climate plan and the electric vehicle sales rule, and keep the carbon price on large industry. Their platform sets no climate target and does not mention the clean fuel rules.
text.5: The Conservatives' October 18 platform would more than double natural gas production by 2032 and triple it by 2035, approve LNG projects and their pipelines, repeal CleanBC 'to remove barriers to investment and growth' while 'keeping a carbon price on large industrial emitters and the revenue it raises', end the zero-emission vehicle sales quota, stop municipal bans on gas connections, and report emissions alongside those avoided through cleaner BC exports. It sets no emissions target and does not mention the Low Carbon Fuel Standard or the 2030 target. The party welcomes the Pacific Link pipeline. In 2024 the party promised to end the carbon tax and the Low Carbon Fuel Standard, and in March 2025 Rustad called the industrial carbon tax 'punishing'.

text.1: This party wants to stop new oil and gas projects and spend on clean power.
text.3: The Greens would stop new fossil fuel development, oppose the oil pipeline, make gas exporters pay for their own power, end fossil fuel subsidies, bring back the rule that all new cars sold be zero-emission by 2035, and fund renewable power and home upgrades. A Green MLA cast the only vote against ending the carbon tax at first reading, and both voted against the fast-track project laws.
text.5: The Greens would stop new fossil fuel development. Their platform and October 10 climate brief would end approvals for new fracking expansion, LNG terminals and expansions and new fossil fuel pipelines, end fossil fuel subsidies, strengthen industrial carbon pricing, set gas royalties at 50% of net profits, end routine methane venting and bring in a binding oil and gas emissions cap if other rules fall short. They oppose the Pacific Link pipeline and would make existing liquefied natural gas plants pay for their own power. They would keep BC's long-term climate targets and add interim ones, restore the rule that all new light-duty vehicles sold be zero-emission by 2035, ban gas hookups in new buildings, offer on-bill financing for home upgrades, restore net metering and aim for electricity to supply at least 35% of energy by 2035 without new large dams. In March 2025 Green MLA Rob Botterell cast the only vote against the carbon tax repeal bill at first reading, and the Greens voted against Bills 14 and 15, which fast-track projects.

text.1: This party says BC will miss its climate goal and wants a lower one in law. It would keep charging big polluters and help homes save energy.
text.3: CentreBC's October 10 platform admits BC will miss its 2030 goal and would set a 20% cut in law instead of 40%. It keeps carbon pricing for large industry with no consumer tax, and adds a methane law, home-upgrade loans, highway chargers and more BC Hydro power. It backs gas exports with First Nations partners and would seek a federal promise in writing to keep the northern tanker ban.
text.5: The platform puts a 2030 milestone of 20% below 2007 in law, down from 40%, keeps the 2040 and 2050 targets and creates a Climate Accountability Office. It keeps industrial carbon pricing, sends at least $100 million a year to the CleanBC Industry Fund and rules out a consumer carbon tax. It would cut methane 75% from 2014 levels by 2030, lend $500 million for 25,000 home upgrades and add 2,000 megawatts of BC Hydro power. It backs net-zero-ready gas exports with First Nations partners and would seek a written federal commitment to keep the northern tanker ban.

text.1: This party wants an oil pipeline to the coast and has no climate plan.
text.3: OneBC would approve a pipeline to Prince Rupert or Kitimat. Beyond general cuts to regulations, it has published no climate commitments and no position on carbon pricing.
text.5: OneBC would build a pipeline to Prince Rupert or Kitimat, scrap the Step Code (a CleanBC energy rule for buildings) and audit 176,000 regulations. It has no climate plan, targets or carbon pricing position, so this quiz places it at the deregulation end by inference.

scoring_rationale: The consumer carbon tax is gone under the NDP, so the live splits are industrial pricing, targets and the pipeline. a = OneBC (4, inferred from its pipeline, Step Code repeal and deregulation items; it has no stated carbon-pricing or target position, so the cell is marked inferred and low confidence); Conservative 2 (shares the pipeline and the CleanBC wind-down, but its October 18 platform keeps the industrial carbon price that this option repeals; score changed Oct 18 after the Conservative platform). b = Conservative platform (4); OneBC 3; NDP 2 (also expands LNG, weakened the EV mandate and keeps industrial pricing, but keeps CleanBC and its conditions); CentreBC 2 (keeps industrial pricing as the option now does and backs conditional LNG and a conditional pipeline, but keeps a legislated target; score changed Oct 18 after option b was rewritten to the Conservative platform). Option b was rewritten on October 18 from 'no commitment on carbon pricing' to the platform text; the other scores on it were kept. c = NDP record (4); CentreBC 3 (same instruments: consumer tax at zero, industrial pricing, net-zero-ready LNG, clean power; differs by legislating a lower 2030 target and adding a methane law); Conservative 2 (consumer tax at zero, industrial pricing and gas growth overlap; it would repeal CleanBC and has no net-zero-ready condition or target; score changed Oct 18 after the Conservative platform) and Green 1. d = Green (4); CentreBC 1 (retrofit loans only); NDP 0 because it is actively expanding LNG. e = CentreBC's platform (4): legislated 20% milestone, industrial pricing kept, methane law, retrofit loans, tanker ban kept; NDP 3 (already runs every instrument in the option and projects the same 20%, but keeps the 40% target in law; its October 13 plan adds the 75% methane cut by 2030 and heat pump rebates, but no legislated 20% milestone or retrofit loans); Conservative 1 (keeps industrial pricing, but would repeal CleanBC and sets no targets or methane rule); Green 2 (keeps the 2040 and 2050 targets and industrial pricing, and adds interim targets, methane cuts and on-bill retrofit financing, but gives none of the option's numbers, no 20% milestone and no tanker-ban line, and rejects LNG; score changed Oct 13 after the Green platform); OneBC 0. Option e was rewritten on October 10 from the July 2026 pipeline conditions to the platform's climate plan; other parties' scores on it were kept. Candidate recruitment is not evidence of policy and is not used.
